events.excerpt: Hi everyone, I’m Maxim from Timeus Lab, the team behind Atomic Launchpad. We’re deploying it to Arbitrum One this week, and before we do, we’d like to introduce it here and hear from delegates. What it is Atomic Launchpad lets anyone launch a token for 0.0005 ETH. Tokens trade on a bonding curve. When the curve fills, it graduates into its own Uniswap v4 pool, and the liquidity position is locked permanently. Two things set it apart: A graduation bar that starts low. For the first 72 hours after deployment, a token graduates at 0.01 ETH raised. After that, the bar rises every 4 hours, up to 4.2 ETH by day 30. Early creators get the cheapest path to a real pool. Creators earn on every trade. Each trade pays a 1% base fee, and a creator can add up to 10% on top, fixed at launch. Creators keep 70% of the fee, and the protocol keeps 30%. Why Arbitrum One DefiLlama lists 11 launchpads on Arbitrum. Together they earned less than $2 in fees over the last 30 days ( DefiLlama , checked October 26). A creator who wants to launch a token on Arbitrum One today has no live place to do it, so they launch on other chains and take their communities with them. events.excerpt: Research & Context The Community Staking Module (CSM) has lowered the financial barrier to staking, allowing permissionless operators to spin up nodes. However, infrastructure centralization remains a silent bottleneck. Due to home bandwidth constraints, power grid instability, or upfront hardware costs, a significant cohort of solo operators choose turn-key hosted infrastructure providers (such as cloud VPS providers) rather than hosting physical hardware at home. While hosted providers lower the technical barrier, they introduce severe correlated infrastructure risks. If a single cloud provider or staking-as-a-service host experiences an outage, a large block of Lido CSM validators could go offline or face correlated slashing penalties simultaneously. Conversely, true home staking provides maximum resilience but suffers from lower uptime SLAs. We need a framework that bridges this gap—improving the accessibility of home infrastructure while structuring guardrails around hosted deployments. The Proposal I propose the creation of a CSM Hybrid Architecture Blueprint & Provider Diversity Framework to optimize the risk profile of permissionless operators. events.headline: Mitigating Correlated Risk: Framework for Hybrid CSM Deployments and Provider Diversity Scoring

events.excerpt: Disclosure: I’m the founder of bb84, the payments app that runs on this chain. Feedback, especially critical feedback, is very welcome. TL;DR We run an OP Stack rollup on Ethereum mainnet (chain ID 42069000, live since 2026-09-30) where L2 transactions carry no signatures at all . An account is the tip of a keccak-256 hash chain. Spending reveals the next preimage. A commit–reveal step binds each preimage to one transaction before the preimage becomes public. Inside the L2 the only cryptographic assumption is preimage resistance of keccak-256, which Grover reduces to about 2^128 work. No known quantum algorithm does better. ECDSA still appears at the L1 boundary, and the system has other trust assumptions (listed below). I’d like to discuss whether this is a sensible interim design for post-quantum payments on Ethereum L2s, and where it breaks. Accounts s_0 = keccak256("OP_OTA_SPEND_v1" ‖ spend_sk ‖ r) // per-account secret s_k = keccak256(s_{k-1}) // k = 1..N, N = 1000 by default C = s_N // public commitment address = trunc20(keccak256("OP_HASH_ADDR_v1" ‖ C)) A predeploy ( NullifierTree , 0x4200…0042) stores per address: lastReveal (initially C ), chainDepth (initially N ) and the set of spent nullifiers. Accounts are registered through an L1 deposit or by the system-side Stealt
events.headline: A hash-only rollup: OP Stack L2 accounts as Lamport-style hash chains, no ECDSA inside the L2

events.excerpt: I recently was bridging a collection of tokens from Cosmos ecosystem with the intent of bringing that liquidity to Stacks. Whilst bridging from many Cosmos chains is very easy, bridging to Stacks is really hard. The “best” route for me was sending everything back into USDC on Arbitrim and Base, sending that to my CEX, swapping to STX, then sending that STX to Stacks. A lot of steps and way too much lost in fees. The USDC from ETH to USDCx on Stacks on AllBridge cost me 0.32 USD of ETH for 2.36 USDC bridged (test tx) and took just over 20 mins. So I didn’t go that route. I’d love to see STX and USDCx get added to a few of the large bridging protocols and make sure they offer good rates. I’m thinking: Across Squid deBridge Also can we get AllBridge to add USDCx swaps to lower fee EVM chains like Base and Arbitrim? Mainnet Ethereum is still the worst (slowest, most expensive) place to transact (after the Bitcoin L1). How can we get that to happen? Is this something the core team at Stacks can work on? 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic

events.excerpt: A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale. So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%. Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests , a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule , and Cloudflare handles the rest. A request for part of a file An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header: GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151 If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range : HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-20
events.headline: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning

events.excerpt: Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography. While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography . Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later. For organizations
events.headline: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management

events.excerpt: The Arbitrum Developer Guild was first introduced in January 2024 alongside the Arbitrum Expansion Program. We have published the first version of the Guild’s specification and it is available in the Arbitrum Foundation’s documentation. The Guild is an invite-only and merit-based program facilitated by the Arbitrum Foundation. Membership is assessed based on demonstrated proof of work on the core Arbitrum Protocol or other high-impact technical contributions to the ecosystem. Members must also demonstrate strong alignment with Arbitrum such that their company’s success substantially depends on Arbitrum winning. The Guild is currently funded through 2% of Net Protocol Revenue from Arbitrum Chains alongside 3% of the Priority Gas Auctions (PGA) and the Sequencer Fast Feed proceeds from Arbitrum One. There are more than 30 Arbitrum Chains who are already contributing to the Guild. Each member will receive an allocated percentage of the funding on a regular cadence. This funding is intended primarily as an additional incentive on top of the member’s core business revenue. With this framework now in place, we are pleased to announce the first member of the Arbitrum Guild: Offchain. Offchain was invited to join the Guild in recognition of their role as the primary architect and maintai

AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. events.excerpt: EIP-8288 proposes recursive aggregation under a fixed protocol-level verification key. One backend choice worth exploring is whether recursive steps should support several approved proof sizes, so that small aggregates can use a smaller proving relation. I implemented this kind of heterogeneous recursion in Parano1d, where small and large recursive state-transition proofs already run on a public mainnet. The construction uses a finite authenticated bank of verifier classes. I recently published the paper , and I think the mechanism is relevant to the aggregation backend being discussed here. Carrying deferred checks across classes A verifier class fixes a relation, its constraint matrix, polynomial commitment parameters and transcript layout. Classes share a public accumulator layout, while their witness dimensions, matrices and commitment geometries can differ. The permitted classes and their ordered bank digest are authenticated public parameters. The part that needs care is deferred verification. Replaying a parent proof leaves a matrix-evaluation claim that must remain accounted for through subsequent recursive steps, including steps using another class. The bank has one accumulator lane per class. At step k , let i_k be the current proof’s class and i_{k-1} its parent’s clas
events.headline: Paranoid EIP-8288: heterogeneous recursion with an authenticated class bank

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, We just opened the public testnet of Luggom, a Cosmos SDK app-chain with one job: turn a real tax payment into money you own, proven end to end with TLSNotary. No KYC. No third parties. The bank session never leaves the user's device. ## Why another chain? Because Cosmos is at its best when an app-chain brings a new kind of user. Luggom brings the taxpayer. There is no subsidy and no token sale. The inflow is a real payment that already leaves people's accounts every year. The chain's job is to prove it happened and mint against it. ## How it works 1. The user pays a real tax at their bank, as always. 2. TLSNotary proves the paid receipt without exposing the session. 3. The notary signs the attestation; the chain verifies it and mints. 4. Each receipt mines exactly once (payment_id + proof_commitment anti-replay). The desktop app (Tauri/Rust) builds the proof request and signs locally. The seed never leaves the device. What is live - chain-id: `luggom-test` - RPC: `https://rpc.luggom.com` - LCD: `https://lcd.luggom.com` - API: `https://api.luggom.com` - Notary: `wss://notary.luggom.com/session` - Full nodes: open (p2p 26656) — seed `1530baa7b3a07e0cab8dc81c9c08fccc51a47471@62.146.183.122:26656` - Validators: by invitation (the operator funds 200 testnet LUG) - App +

events.excerpt: Hi all, Thanks to @aelowsson @julian @b-wagn @GottfriedHerold , since this builds directly on LUCID, the criticism thread and the ticket-first threshold IBE design. Also a kind request for review on this work. I’ve been wondering how much the “free option” in encrypted mempools is actually worth, and what happens if you try to take it away. The short version is in the TL;DR. The full treatment, with proofs, is in the paper, and the Lean 4 formalization is linked below. Edit (Oct 28): BSR is now instantiated on Gottfried’s ticket-first threshold IBE design, and the timing numbers are corrected for the ePBS bid commitment. Details in the reply below. TL;DR If a sender can decide whether to reveal after seeing new information, they hold a free option. I bound its value and show what happens when you try to remove it. Fees alone don’t price it well, because senders can use many conditional commitments. Taking the option from senders just moves it to committee members. I propose Blind Simultaneous Release (BSR), which fixes the executed set before anyone can condition on new information. It uses only hashes, so it is post-quantum. It plugs into the ticket-first threshold IBE design as a release layer for the committee’s key shares. Paper: Reveal-Optionality-BSR.pdf (395.8 KB), or you
events.headline: Reveal optionality in encrypted mempools: how big is the sender’s free option, and a post-quantum way to remove it
